article_text:
The Pasifika Entertainment Advancement Komiti has named the third cohort of its annual PEAK Writers Fellowship.

This year’s cohort includes Kanani Koster, Erin Lau, Sean Oketani, Neil Tinkham and Pouariʻi Tanne. Supported by Netflix, the fellowship selects five up-and-coming writers whose work honors Pasifika (people of Pacific Islander descent) experiences, providing them with mentorship, professional development and networking opportunities as they continue to expand their professional television careers.

Related Stories

‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Confirms Universal Wavered in Planning Overseas Release, Says He Tried to Interview Elon Musk: ‘His Response Was Writing “Gibney Is a Douche”’

Korea Box Office: Anime Feature 'Chiikawa' Edges Past 'The Assassin(s)' to Claim Weekend Crown

Founded by PEAK co-founder, director, screenwriter and showrunner Dana Ledoux Miller and co-managed by program manager and screenwriter Bryson Chun, the fellowship serves as the only Hollywood writing program created by a Pasifika storyteller.

“I’m so grateful that in this time of industry uncertainty, Netflix continues to invest in emerging writers,” Miller said. “Fellowships like this not only make it possible for our communities to steward our own stories from script to screen, they allow the five incredible writers in this year’s fellowship to challenge and upend expectations of who we are expected to be as artists.”

Each fellow is paired with an experienced industry mentor who helps refine their scripts to be professionally presented. Also included in the fellowship are weekly panels and conversations with writers, showrunners, executives, representatives, actors and other industry professionals, offering insight on the entertainment industry.

This year’s fellows will receive mentorship from Ryan Belezon and Jeffrey Gelber (“Boulevard”); Aminta Goyel (“Pivoting”); Lauren Thompson (“Ghostwriter”); and Michelle Giannusa (“Ripple”).

“We received a record number of applications this year, which shows how sorely this fellowship is needed,” said Averie Huffine, the interim executive director of PEAK. “But I think it’s also due to Netflix being synonymous with great programming, and the reputation of Dana and Bryson’s incredible mentorship.”

See the list of fellows below.

Kanani Koster — “ Clinic Daze”

A half-hour dramedy following the ragtag yet passionate staff of an underfunded abortion clinic hustling to provide compassionate care to their patients, all while navigating their own chaotic personal lives.

Koster is a native Hawaiian writer and director. Her work uses raunchy blue comedy to hide a desire to make a difference in this world. Kanani is a 2024 American Film Institute directing alum, 2024 ‘Ohina Lab Fellow and ‘23 Punky Aloha Scholar for Kanaka ‘Ōiwi and Pasifika Creatives. Her work has been supported by the Tribeca Film Festival, Gotham’s Project Market, Visionary Justice Story Lab and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Her shorts have played at AFI Fest, SeriesFest, Hawai’i International Film Festival, and the Smithsonian Museum.

Erin Lau — “The Hālau ”

“The Hālau” is a one-hour family drama that follows 16-year-old Maile Johnson who, after her mother’s death, is forced to live with her estranged family on Oahu and enter the world of competitive hula dancing.

The Native Hawaiian filmmaker explores empathy, redemption and legacy through her work. She has been supported by the Sundance Institute, Tribeca Studios, Film Independent, Ryan Murphy’s Half Initiative and more. Her work spans narrative, documentary and episodic storytelling and has been featured on the Criterion Channel, Netflix and PBS.Lu’s most recent directing credit was for Fox’s action-packed procedural “Rescue: HI-Surf.” She is also currently a fellow in the 2026 ImagineNATIVE Screenwriting Series Lab and the Sundance Institute | The Asian American Foundation (TAAF) Accelerator.

Sean Oketani — “[Pair]adise”

Two queer, hapa Hawaiian best friends decide to ditch their jobs as hotel servers and spend the day playing tourists in Waikīkī.

Oketani is a Native Hawaiian writer, director and storyteller born and raised on the island of Oʻahu. He graduated from Chapman University’s Dodge College of Film and Media Arts with a BFA in television writing and production. He wrote and produced his undergraduate thesis, “Gay Church,” a short-form comedy pilot. He has worked across the programming, education, and outreach departments at the Hawaiʻi International Film Festival (HIFF). In 2025, he was selected as an ʻOhina Labs Writers Fellow and received the ʻOhina Judge’s Award for his short film script, currently in pre-production.

His work often draws from the intersection of his identities and perspectives, navigating both lived and inherited experiences. He is passionate about crafting compelling narratives that explore the contradictions and overlaps of identity, culture and belonging. He is inspired by Indigenous and Pasifika cinema; queer art and literature; and the influence of digital culture, both on and offline.

Neil Tinkham — “West Coast Chamorus ”

A straight-laced Chamoru father must confront his past as a gangbanger when he returns to Los Angeles with his son for medical treatment.

Tinkham is a Chamoru filmmaker originally from Guam. His work reflects his island upbringing and the Chamoru diaspora community. His short movies have received funding from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, the Pacific Islanders in Communications and the Guam Council for the Arts and Humanities Agency. His work has screened at film festivals and regional museums and received distribution. In 2018, Neil’s feature-length screenplay “Jungle ” was optioned by New Zealand-based production company Popgun Filmmakers, and, in 2022, his screenplay “The Taotaomona” was selected for the Second Annual Indigenous List, compiled by the Sundance Institute, ImagineNative and The Black List. Other scripts Tinkham has written have placed in screenwriting labs and competitions, including the Ohina Filmmakers Lab and the Page International Screenwriting Awards.

Pouariʻi Tanner — “The Assistant”

When a Māori current affairs crew arrives in Hollywood to profile its Indigenous stars, they discover their promised access doesn’t exist and must navigate the assistants, gatekeepers and strange characters operating behind the scenes of the Indigenous entertainment industry.

Tanner is a Cook Islands writer and producer based in Rarotonga. Her work draws on her experience across Indigenous film, television and media, using comedy and character-driven storytelling to explore the strange intersections between island communities and larger cultural institutions. She previously worked with the Sundance Institute’s Indigenous Program and created and produced the documentary series “Turtle Town” in the Cook Islands. She is currently developing three short films through Pasifika TV’s film masterclass, to be completed and released in 2027. Through her production company, Pacific Standard Time, she is developing original film and television projects from the Pacific.

"展览的官方说明宣称，劳森无意对这些图像做道德评判，而是“将代理权的内涵以及美妆产品在我们晚期资本主义社会中的变革潜力置于核心地位”。劳森并非试图将这些行窃者妖魔化或美化，但她确实在保护他们。行窃者的照片具有模糊性——原始图像分辨率较低，部分行窃者戴着面具，还有几张照片极其模糊，以至于观者根本无法辨认出拍摄对象的面孔。劳森刻意拒绝将这些图像变得清晰，促使观者去思考他们究竟在看什么、或者在看谁。谁是普通顾客，谁又是罪犯？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她通过做出一种艺术抉择，即让拍摄对象与那些形象并非采集自监控摄像头的其他黑人形成鲜明对比，从而在对拍摄对象的描绘中追求一种中立性。在劳森行窃者照片正对面的右侧墙上，悬挂着这位摄影师标志性风格的肖像：那是黑人在极其私密的环境中生活状态丰富饱满的图像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在所有这些艺术作品中，拍摄对象的凝视总是与观者的目光相遇，从而强化了他们的人性并拉平了权力关系。事实上，由于尺幅巨大，拍摄对象似乎正居高临下地看着你。在20世纪早期，黑人摄影师会将身着西装、修女服或毕业长袍的黑人拍摄对象永恒定格，以此将一种新型的种族骄傲与体面引入主流。劳森的拍摄对象则穿着随意——如果穿了衣服的话。她所关心的并不是某种尊严式的黑人性，而是在平凡日常中黑人性的美。通过将所有这些图像并置于同一空间，劳森迫使观者透过充满种种矛盾的生活连续体来看待黑人性，而不是将其简化为好与坏行为的扁平二元对立。", "links": [{"text": "Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjects", "url": "https://time.com/5539596/early-african-american-photographers/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "房间两侧黑人拍摄对象之间的关系，取决于观者自身的判断。辫子接发过道附近的那个黑人女性行窃者，与那个双膝分开蹲着的裸体黑人女性有多大区别？那个黑人男性行窃者，与那个眼睛受伤、在起居室里与他人一起摆姿势的黑人男人有多大区别？观者如何评价这些拍摄对象，恰恰暴露了他们自身的偏见。但在这次展览中，个人的偏见并非私密且无关紧要的瑕疵，而是必须直面的意识形态束缚。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《边境控制》（Edge Control）成功捕捉了那些在追求美的过程中在不知情下被监控的人们的极度脆弱。与此同时，劳森缩小了旁观者与参与者之间的差距，因为观者面对的是多重的凝视——包括他们自己的凝视——从而使任何个人的价值都不会被区别对待。随着权力的短暂重构，平等得以实现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "《边境控制》（Edge Control）在纽约高古轩画廊展出，展期至10月24日。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
In her essay The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators, writer and philosopher bell hooks explains that the relationship between Black people and the act of “looking” has been traumatic since slavery. Black people, many of whom are still subject to the constant surveillance that originated during enslavement, have historically been punished with severe consequences, such as lynching, for looking back at those who subjugate them. Despite these risks, hooks writes, they rebelled by secretly looking at white people, as well as their surroundings, rejecting the white gaze as the singular framework of reality. We can, as bell hooks writes, “interrogate the gaze of the Other but also look back, and at one another, naming what we see”.

I thought of this analysis when I visited Edge Control, artist Deana Lawson’s latest photography exhibition at the Gagosian gallery in New York City. Edge control refers to the gels and pomades that slick the hairs along the edges of a Black woman’s hairline, but in Lawson’s exhibit, the phrase takes on an additional meaning. It’s at once a styling product for Black haircare devotees as well as a tool to examine the beauty industry, consumerism and how surveillance and race intersect.

To explore these intersections, Lawson uses photos of alleged beauty supply store shoplifters, presented in large scale and outside their original contexts. As a warning to customers, many beauty supply stores post surveillance photos of alleged shoplifters caught in the act of stealing products. The stores, which almost exclusively sell Black haircare products within Black neighborhoods, are rarely owned by Black people. The small, indistinct images tend to fade in the background amid the various colors of shampoo bottles and hair accessories.

Lawson’s images, however, are large portraits framed by mirrors, forcing the onlooker to simultaneously see themselves looking at these shoplifters. The viewer is small and narrow while the shoplifters are life-size, and what was once quiet, passive spectatorship immediately becomes active participation. This evolution is further emphasized once a viewer moves to the middle of the gallery room where two holograms stand, revealing Black women’s bodies that shift depending on the viewer’s angle. These pieces demonstrate how Lawson manipulates perception: these alleged shoplifters are not frozen in time, they are in motion, just as the viewers are.

The notion of wrongdoing is questionable as the exhibition becomes a house of mirrors exploring who is and is not being watched. Lawson accomplishes exactly what bell hooks wrote about – the rebellious gaze – by looking at her subjects, challenging viewers to evaluate them, and therefore exploring how perception functions within a space full of unequal power relations.

The exhibit’s official description proclaims that Lawson does not intend to cast moral judgment over these images, but rather “foregrounds the implications of agency and transformative potential of beauty products within our late capitalist society”. Lawson is not trying to villainize or glorify these shoplifters, but she does protect them. The shoplifter photos are evasive – the original images are low resolution, some of the shoplifters are masked and a few of the photos are so blurry that the viewer is unable to make out the subject’s face. Lawson’s deliberate refusal to clarify these images causes the viewer to contemplate what or who they are looking at. Who is the regular customer and who is the criminal?

She aims for neutrality in the depiction of her subjects by making the artistic decision to show them in stark contrast to other Black people whose images were not gathered from surveillance cameras. On the right wall opposite Lawson’s shoplifter images, the photographer’s signature style portraits hang: lush images of Black men and women in very private settings.

In all these artworks, the subjects’ gaze always meets the viewers’, reinforcing their humanity and leveling the playing field. In fact, due to their size, the subjects seem to be looking down at you. In the early 20th century, Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjects in suits, nuns’ habits or graduate gowns to usher in a new form of race pride – and respectability – into the mainstream. Lawson’s subjects are casually dressed – if at all. She’s not interested in a dignified kind of Blackness, but rather the beauty of Blackness within the mundane. By placing all of these images together within the same space, Lawson forces the viewers to view Blackness through a continuum of life in all of its contradictions, rather than a flat binary of good and bad behavior.

The relationship between the Black subjects on both sides of the room is contingent upon the viewer’s own judgment. How different is the Black female shoplifter near the braid extensions aisle from the naked Black woman squatting with her knees apart? How different is the Black male shoplifter from the Black man with a busted eye posing with others in a living room? However the viewer judges these subjects reveals their own biases. But in this exhibition, one’s biases are not private, inconsequential flaws. They’re ideological constraints that must be confronted.

Edge Control succeeds at capturing the extreme vulnerability of people who are being surveilled without their knowledge in active pursuit of beauty. At the same time, Lawson narrows the gap between spectator and participant as the viewer is confronted with multiple gazes–including their own–so that no one person is valued differently than the other. With power being briefly reassembled, parity is achieved.

Edge Control is on view at the Gagosian in New York City until 24 October

article_text:
Guide

7 New York Exhibitions That Embody Indigenous Survivance

In shows coinciding with Indigenous Peoples' Day, artists including Jeremy Dennis, Shelley Niro, and Sarah Sense chart Native history and futurity.

To commemorate Indigenous Peoples' Day here in New York, we have highlighted seven ongoing exhibitions of Native art and history in Manhattan, the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College, and the Long Island Museum in Stony Brook. Across solo and group presentations, the featured artists, who represent a diverse tapestry of Indigenous populations across Turtle Island, embody survivance by tracing and rejecting narratives of dispossession and irrelevance, upending and satirizing stereotypes, preserving and reinventing traditional art forms, and bringing underrepresented histories out from the margins.

Some of these sites are closed in observance of the occasion, and some of you have not been afforded the three-day weekend commanding this period of reflection, so rest assured that the following programs will be available from the last week of October through next spring.

Cannupa Hanska Luger: American Traditional

Garth Greenan Gallery , 10 Greene Street, SoHo, Manhattan Through Oct. 24

Inaugurating the gallery's new space, Cannupa Hanska Luger's (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara, and Lakota) American Traditional exchanges the artist's typically colorful verve for a series of uniform matte-black works born from ironstone clay, sumi ink, and direct flame. The titular work presents a striated sculpture of a skinned bison with a bifurcated skull sitting on a standard colonial-fashion dining table. Encoded in tautly wrapped yarn, this distortion manifests throughout Luger's wall hangings and pedestals of other animal skulls and carcasses, which are embellished with railroad spikes, Pulaski axes, and vintage “American Traditional” furniture associated with the westward settler expansion. Per the artist, the work emphasizes the “bizarre and horrific history of colonialism,” and the motifs of mutilation and mutation speak to the manipulation of collective memory in the retelling and neglect of certain perspectives.

Shelley Niro: In Her Lifetime

Hales Gallery , 547 West 20th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan Through Oct. 31

Turtle Clan of the Kanyen’kehá:ka (Mohawk) Nation artist and filmmaker Shelley Niro celebrates her second solo show with Hales New York in a tight selection of mixed-media photographic works spanning decades of her career. In Her Lifetime , which takes its name from Niro's 1992 black-and-white picture sequence of her sister with overlaid text, emphasizes the artist's use of humor and accessible references in her personal reflections on identity, nationhood, collective memory, and stereotypes through an Indigenous perspective. For this exhibition, Niro also reinterprets a variety of her iconic photos from the early 1990s, embellishing them with hand-painted elements and decorative patterns that, in the context of Indigenous womanhood, add a certain cheeky assertiveness to her family portrayals.

Sarah Sense: Land, Line, Blood, Memory

Bruce Silverstein Gallery , 529 West 20th Street (4th Floor), Chelsea, Manhattan Through Nov. 21

Chitimacha/Choctaw artist Sarah Sense’s latest series frames traditional rivercane basket weaving as a restorative practice, one that reconnects her with her ancestry and cultural traditions while creating a tangible heirloom for future generations. Sense weaves photographs taken at national parks and other significant landscapes printed on rice and bamboo paper together with colonial documents pertaining to Native land dispossession — such as maps and treaties — to create multi-dimensional compositions that reunite historic Indigenous art and stewardship practices with the environments integral to their formations. Sense deliberately undercuts colonial authority by manipulating these settler-driven documents.

article_text:
Cynthia Erivo is rounding out her cast of magical beings with the latest Bad Fairies news, which announced live on Thursday at the Hollywood Bowl.

During her one-night-only concert Let Me Sing to You , the 2x Grammy winner revealed that Kylie Minogue , Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate have joined her in the cast of the Warner Bros./Locksmith animated musical comedy, which is scheduled to premiere May 21, 2027 in theaters, in addition to teasing an orchestral arrangement of her character Jayne’s song “Hard to Believe”.

Minogue will voice Clowder, the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow, and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother. They join Cynthia Erivo, who leads the film as Jayne Staplegun.

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo To Star In Animated Musical ‘Bad Fairies’ For Warner Bros. Animation And Locksmith Animation

Ncuti Gatwa Joins Cynthia Erivo In ‘Bad Fairies’ Animated Musical Cast

Minogue, who was in attendance at Thursday’s show, said in a statement, “I’m so excited to be part of Bad Fairies , alongside the incredible Cynthia Erivo, Jonathan Groff and such a brilliant cast of voices. And getting to play both a cat and a witch? It’s a little bit magical, a little bit mischievous and a whole lot of fun.”

Watch on Deadline

Directed by Megan Nicole Dong and co-directed by Olivier Staphylas, Bad Fairies is an original musical comedy set in contemporary London that follows a delightfully subversive gang of fairies as they shake up their magical world. The film is penned by Deborah Frances-White.

Previously announced cast includes Serrana Su-Ling Bliss as Fei Chang, James Acaster as Stickers, Dee Bradley Baker as Groundbeef and Ncuti Gatwa as Butterwort.

Tony-winning duo Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss ( Six: The Musical ) are writing original songs, with Grammy-nominated Isabella “Machine” Summers (Florence + The Machine) composing the score and contributing to the songs. Ian Eisendrath ( KPop Demon Hunters ) serves as executive music producer.

Kylie Minogue is represented by Jason Weinberg at Untitled and Polly Bhowmik at Context Management. Jonathan Groff is represented by Brian Boone and Joe Michota at CAA. Catherine Tate is represented by Jeremy Barber at UTA and Robert Taylor at The Artists Partnership.
